description: Pilar Karya is an interdisciplinary team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 (Purwokerto). We focus on the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge, exploring lunar open data and environmental parameters at the Lunar South Pole to support Artemis operations.
summary: XASUAI is a formula-based lunar mission planning platform and simulation assistant designed to streamline the 3-step lunar landing journey by reducing mission planning complexity and mitigating environmental uncertainties. The platform integrates three core features: the Smart Landing Planner, which determines optimal landing locations and times based on lunar conditions; the Lunar Terrain Explorer, which provides interactive 2D and 3D visual assets to simplify surface analysis; and the Lunar Mission Simulator, which models spacecraft trajectories and landing processes from Earth to the Moon using rigorous calculations. By implementing systematic formulas for environmental analysis and trajectory simulation, XASUAI eliminates guesswork, enhances decision-making accuracy, and ensures safer, more effective lunar landing missions.
details:
XASUAI is a lunar mission navigation system developed to help determine optimal landing sites and launch windows for Artemis spacecraft at Mons Mouton, located in the lunar South Pole region. The system evaluates environmental conditions, lunar surface topography, and spacecraft dynamics to support safe and controlled landing mission planning.

Landing in the lunar South Pole region presents three major aerospace engineering challenges: extreme environmental conditions, rugged surface topography, and spacecraft dynamics during the landing process.

The first challenge is the extreme environment. At the lunar South Pole, both the Sun and Earth appear at very low angles above the horizon. These conditions limit solar energy availability and direct communication with Earth. Temperatures can also reach as low as -240°C, potentially threatening spacecraft electrical systems. To address these challenges, XASUAI provides the Landing Schedule Recommendation feature. The system tracks the ephemerides of the Sun and Earth to identify mission windows that offer sustained solar illumination and direct line-of-sight communication with Earth.

The second challenge is uneven surface topography. The area surrounding Mons Mouton contains steep crater slopes and permanently shadowed regions. Landing on surfaces with excessive slopes may cause spacecraft instability, while surrounding crater ridges can obstruct communication between onboard antennas and Earth. To address this challenge, XASUAI provides the Topography Visualization and Analysis feature. It displays two-dimensional contour maps, three-dimensional terrain visualizations, and horizon profiles to examine surface conditions around Mons Mouton. Terrain gradient analysis is used to assess the suitability of potential landing areas, while horizon profile analysis helps identify obstructions along antenna line-of-sight paths.

The third challenge involves spacecraft dynamics. A spacecraft traveling at an orbital velocity of approximately 1.7 km/s requires controlled deceleration before reaching the lunar surface. Guidance errors during this process may result in inefficient propellant consumption or increase the risk of a hazardous landing impact. To address this challenge, XASUAI provides the Flight and Landing Simulation feature. The system simulates six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) flight dynamics, engine thrust control, and propellant management. The simulation runs in real time to evaluate descent behavior, spacecraft attitude stability, and remaining propellant throughout the landing process, with the objective of achieving a controlled vertical touchdown.

These three solutions are integrated into a mission workflow consisting of three stages. The first stage is Recommendation, which uses a Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) approach to analyze the ephemerides of the Sun and Earth, along with elevation profiles, over a 336-hour period. This analysis utilizes NASA JPL Horizons data and the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) Digital Elevation Model (DEM) to calculate scores across multiple criteria and identify landing windows with favorable illumination and Earth visibility conditions.

The second stage is Visualization, which allows users to examine lunar surface conditions through two-dimensional and three-dimensional topographic visualizations, as well as horizon profiles. Users can explore terrain characteristics, inspect the slopes of potential landing areas, and identify possible physical obstructions along antenna communication paths. This stage also includes an interactive two-dimensional geospatial map for displaying the coordinates of Mons Mouton and the areas being analyzed.

The third stage is Simulation, which evaluates landing dynamics through a three-dimensional flight simulation. By applying a six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) flight dynamics model and Artemis spacecraft orbital mechanics, the system evaluates controlled descent, spacecraft attitude stability, engine thrust control, and propellant availability throughout the landing process.

Overall, XASUAI integrates landing window recommendations, terrain analysis, and flight dynamics simulation into a unified lunar mission navigation system. The platform is designed to help users understand the factors influencing landing site and launch window selection, examine lunar surface conditions, and explore spacecraft landing procedures through interactive simulations.

XASUAI utilizes data and resources from NASA, including NASA JPL Horizons for obtaining ephemeris data and the NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) LOLA Digital Elevation Model for acquiring lunar surface elevation information. These datasets form the foundation for landing window analysis and topographic visualization of Mons Mouton. Previously retrieved LOLA elevation data and ephemeris data are also stored locally, allowing the system to reuse them when needed.

XASUAI is developed using Python, JavaScript, HTML5, and CSS3 as its primary programming languages. The system supports two operating modes: a web-based application and a desktop application. In web mode, the backend is built using the Tornado framework, which supports asynchronous processing. Two-dimensional geospatial mapping is implemented using Leaflet.js, while three-dimensional terrain visualization and flight simulation are powered by Three.js and WebGL. In desktop mode, the system provides a native interface built with PyQt6 and uses PyQtGraph for real-time telemetry graph rendering. Numerical computations, terrain slope analysis, and trajectory integration using the fourth/fifth-order Runge-Kutta method (RK45) are supported by the NumPy and SciPy libraries. Source code management and development collaboration are handled through Git and GitHub.

XASUAI is designed to run on standard laptops and desktop computers without requiring specialized aerospace hardware. The system requires Python version 3.10 or later. The web application requires a modern browser with WebGL support, while the desktop application runs in a PyQt6-based environment. A modern multi-core processor and at least 4 GB of RAM are recommended as baseline hardware specifications.

One of XASUAI's key capabilities is its local data storage mechanism (offline caching), which uses the horizons_cache.json file and locally available LOLA elevation data. This mechanism allows the system to reuse previously stored datasets, enabling features that rely on this information to remain accessible without an internet connection. An internet connection is only required when users need to retrieve or update astronomical data directly from external sources through live data fetching. Therefore, the system's operation does not entirely depend on continuous internet connectivity.

As a prototype, XASUAI is intended for educational, analytical, and exploratory purposes related to lunar landing mission planning. Its analytical and simulation results depend on the datasets, assumptions, and computational models implemented in the system. Therefore, XASUAI should not be considered a validated flight navigation system for actual space missions.
